From "If it is correct" onwards, this clarifies the functional efficacy, which is divided into two parts: first, clarifying how it destroys desire and assists the correct [path], which is further divided into two: first, a brief indication; second, an extensive indication, which is divided into three: first, citing the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Shèlùn) to clarify how it assists the correct [path]. Regarding the "three liberations": [The text continues: ...the three gates of liberation are: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Emptiness-liberation is the gate of liberation through the contemplation of emptiness; signlessness-liberation is the gate of liberation through the contemplation of signlessness; wishlessness-liberation is the gate of liberation through the contemplation of wishlessness. These three gates of liberation are able to sever all afflictions and exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*). Why is this? Because these three gates of liberation are the antidotes to the three poisons. Specifically, emptiness-liberation is the antidote to the poison of greed; signlessness-liberation is the antidote to the poison of hatred; wishlessness-liberation is the antidote to the poison of delusion. Furthermore, these three gates of liberation are able to sever the three fetters. Specifically, emptiness-liberation severs the fetter of views; signlessness-liberation severs the fetter of grasping at precepts and observances; wishlessness-liberation severs the fetter of doubt. Furthermore, these three gates of liberation are able to sever the three poisons and exhaust the four nutriments. Specifically, emptiness-liberation severs the poison of greed and exhausts the nutriment of contact; signlessness-liberation severs the poison of hatred and exhausts the nutriment of volitional formations; wishlessness-liberation severs the poison of delusion and exhausts the nutriment of consciousness. Furthermore, these three gates of liberation are able to sever the three poisons and exhaust the five aggregates. Specifically, emptiness-liberation severs the poison of greed and exhausts the aggregate of form; signlessness-liberation severs the poison of hatred and exhausts the aggregate of perception; wishlessness-liberation severs the poison of delusion and exhausts the aggregates of feeling, volition, and consciousness. Furthermore, these three gates of liberation are able to sever the three poisons and exhaust the six sense bases. Specifically, emptiness-liberation severs the poison of greed and exhausts the sense base of the eye; signlessness-liberation severs the poison of hatred and exhausts the sense base of the ear; wishlessness-liberation severs the poison of delusion and exhausts the sense bases of the nose, tongue, body, and mind. Furthermore, these three gates of liberation are able to sever the three poisons and exhaust the seven stations of consciousness. Specifically, emptiness-liberation severs the poison of greed and exhausts the station of consciousness in the realm of infinite space; signlessness-liberation severs the poison of hatred and exhausts the station of consciousness in the realm of infinite consciousness; wishlessness-liberation severs the poison of delusion and exhausts the station of consciousness in the realm of nothingness. Furthermore, these three gates of liberation are able to sever the three poisons and exhaust the nine successive abodes. Specifically, emptiness-liberation severs the poison of greed and exhausts the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas; signlessness-liberation severs the poison of hatred and exhausts the realm of infinite space and the realm of infinite consciousness; wishlessness-liberation severs the poison of delusion and exhausts the realm of nothingness and the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Furthermore, these three gates of liberation are able to sever the three poisons and exhaust the ten stages of wholesome roots. Specifically, emptiness-liberation severs the poison of greed and exhausts the stage of patience; signlessness-liberation severs the poison of hatred and exhausts the stage of the summit of existence; wishlessness-liberation severs the poison of delusion and exhausts the stage of the worldly-first-dharma. Furthermore, these three gates of liberation are able to sever the three poisons and exhaust the eleven knowledges. Specifically, emptiness-liberation severs the poison of greed and exhausts the knowledge of suffering; signlessness-liberation severs the poison of hatred and exhausts the knowledge of origination; wishlessness-liberation severs the poison of delusion and exhausts the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path. Furthermore, these three gates of liberation are able to sever the three poisons and exhaust the twelve links of dependent origination. Specifically, emptiness-liberation severs the poison of greed and exhausts ignorance, volitional formations, and craving; signlessness-liberation severs the poison of hatred and exhausts consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling; wishlessness-liberation severs the poison of delusion and exhausts clinging, becoming, birth, and old age-and-death. Furthermore, these three gates of liberation are able to sever the three poisons and exhaust the eighteen elements. Specifically, emptiness-liberation severs the poison of greed and exhausts the element of the eye and the element of forms; signlessness-liberation severs the poison of hatred and exhausts the element of the ear and the element of sounds; wishlessness-liberation severs the poison of delusion and exhausts the elements of the nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as the elements of odors, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena. Furthermore, these three gates of liberation are able to sever the three poisons and exhaust the twenty-two faculties. Specifically, emptiness-liberation severs the poison of greed and exhausts the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, life, mind, pleasure, joy, equanimity, faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; signlessness-liberation severs the poison of hatred and exhausts the faculty of masculinity and the faculty of femininity; wishlessness-liberation severs the poison of delusion and exhausts the faculty of suffering, the faculty of grief, the faculty of bodily sensation, the faculty of view, the faculty of wrong resolve, the faculty of doubt, and the faculty of ignorance. Furthermore, these three gates of liberation are able to sever the three poisons and exhaust the twenty-four aspects. Specifically, emptiness-liberation severs the poison of greed and exhausts the aspect of impermanence, the aspect of suffering, the aspect of emptiness, and the aspect of non-self; signlessness-liberation severs the poison of hatred and exhausts the aspect of tranquility, the aspect of sublime, the aspect of detachment, and the aspect of cessation; wishlessness-liberation severs the poison of delusion and exhausts the aspect of dispassion, the aspect of extinction, the aspect of stillness, and the aspect of relinquishment. Furthermore, these three gates of liberation are able to sever the three poisons and exhaust the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. Specifically, emptiness-liberation severs the poison of greed and exhausts the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five These are emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; arising from the threefold realization of the fruit, they are called the gates of liberation.
Liberation and nirvana are two names for a single essence.

Regarding the "Dharmapada" as the method for opening the gates: in the Hinayana, the sixteen aspects of contemplation constitute the three gates of liberation; in this present chapter, however, emptiness, the provisional, and the middle are taken as the three gates of liberation.

If one wishes for this gate to open, one must cultivate it by means of testing and training through the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*). Just as one cultivates the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) in terms of emptiness, provisional existence, and the middle way, so too is it with the four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*) and up to the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*); the method of testing and training is likewise the same.
The three liberations of the Hīnayāna and the seven categories of training are likewise in this sense; all take the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) as their method of opening the door.

As for the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*): first, the perception of bloating; second, the perception of decay; third, the perception of being smeared with blood; fourth, the perception of festering pus; fifth, the perception of bluish discoloration; sixth, the perception of being devoured; seventh, the perception of scattering; eighth, the perception of bones; and ninth, the perception of burning.
If categorized according to the Hīnayāna, there are two types of persons:
first, those who destroy the Dharma, who seek only the cessation of suffering; they proceed as far as the perception of burning and become persons liberated by wisdom (prajñā-vimukta).

Second, those who do not destroy the Dharma abide in the contemplation of the skeleton but do not advance to the contemplation of burning; they attain the full complement of merits such as the emission of radiant light and become persons liberated in both ways.

Now it is explained that when a bodhisattva perceives the true reality (*dharmatā*) of dhyāna, it is called "cultivating penetrating dhyāna" (*prativedha-dhyāna*), which is forever distinct from that of the Lesser Vehicle.
Although the Greater and Lesser Vehicles differ, both employ the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) as an aid to opening the three gates of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*).
Within the section on "Aids to Opening," the nine perceptions of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*) break the vanguard of desire; therefore, they are called the "initial gateway.
Second, it demonstrates that the power of the clarity gained through progressive cultivation is great:
one first cultivates the perception of impurity, then enters the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*) and the great perception of impurity.

Regarding what is called "great," observing only one's own and others' primary retribution (the body) is termed "small impurity," which refers to the nine contemplations of loathsomeness (*navasaṃjñā*).

If one observes both the primary and secondary retribution (the environment), it is termed "great impurity. This means: viewing houses as burial mounds, money as dead snakes, soup as excrement broth, rice as white worms, clothing as stinking hides, mountains as heaps of flesh, ponds as rivers of pus, gardens and groves as withered bones, and rivers and seas as pouring filth—this is called great impurity.

It is also called the "Great Liberation" (*mahā-vimokṣa*). "Turning one's back" (*pratyudāvarta*) means turning one's back on these pure five desires; "relinquishing" (*tyāga*) means relinquishing this mind of attachment.
Third, citing the *Mahā-sūtra* to clarify the treatment of desire and the attainment of liberation.
Observation has a powerful counteractive force and swiftly gives rise to the untainted (anāsrava).
Second, from "This is not... onwards, it clarifies how the two emptinesses assist the primary [practice], in three parts:
first, a general indication based on the meaning.
2. Quotation of Scripture for Specific Demonstration.
Regarding the "eightfold colored light rays," these refer to the eight kinds of colors: earth, water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, and white.

The *Dharmadhātu-krama* states: "One sees the color of earth as ground that is yellowish-white and pure; one sees the color of water as water as clear as a deep abyss; one sees the color of fire as smokeless and pure fire; one sees the color of wind as dustless and far-reaching, pristine wind; one sees the color blue as a mountain of refined gold; one sees the color yellow as a *campaka* flower; one sees the color red as the dawn clouds of spring; and one sees the color white as conch shells and snow."
3. From "This refers to" below, the conclusion establishes the auxiliary as supporting the primary.

Because one cultivates the dhyāna of phenomena (*vastu-dhyāna*) to counteract desire, and because one realizes through the correct contemplation of the two emptinesses that the impure object is the *dharmadhātu*, one perceives neither a provisional person nor real dharmas within the bones or the light.

When this primary practice and its auxiliary are cultivated in combination, it constitutes the Mahāyāna method for opening [the path] through auxiliaries. Second, the establishment of the doctrine in three parts:
First, clarifying that the Truths and Conditions are the root of the Great [Vehicle], in two parts:
First, clarifying the penetration of the Great [Vehicle], in four parts:
first, a question concerning the exclusive Small [Vehicle].
Now that you speak of the perfect emptiness, how can you instead employ the Four Noble Truths of the Śrāvakas and the Dependent Origination of the Pratyekabuddhas?
Second, answering by way of the general Mahāyāna:
The Buddha’s teaching on the Truths and Conditions applies universally to both the Great and Small Vehicles and to Bodhisattvas, as it encompasses all four teachings.
It is like a great public road upon which all classes of people travel together; it does not belong exclusively to the small.
3. The repeated question:
namely, the four characters "What is the general meaning? (tō-i kanyo).
4. From "Nirvana" downward, the extensive explanation, in two parts:
First, the general clarification of the Four Noble Truths.

Regarding the phrase "In the past, etc.": when the Buddha and those of the three vehicles were formerly ordinary beings, they did not perceive the true reality of the fourfold Four Noble Truths; therefore, they continued to transmigrate through the birth-and-death of the segmented realm (*prātibhajika-saṃsāra*).
The verse has not yet been completed; I shall now cite it in full, hence the annotation "and so forth.

As for the statement that ordinary beings have suffering but no Truth (satya), it means that although they encounter great suffering, they do not regard it as a calamity, because they lack the discernment to realize it as suffering.

Śrāvakas experience suffering and possess the Truth of Suffering; because they do not understand non-arising within the Tripitaka, it is said that they "possess suffering," yet because they can discern and know it, it is called the "Truth of Suffering."

Regarding the phrase "Bodhisattvas and others," this refers to those who, across all three teachings, equally realize that all things are like illusions and are thus able to understand suffering such that it is non-existent in its very place.

As for the mention of "the True Truth" (*satya*), Master Zhāng'ān’s commentary states: "Because 'True' means 'genuinely real,' this refers to the two kinds of reality—both sequential and non-sequential."
Regarding "the Buddhas and so forth": the fruit of Buddhahood is perfectly consummate and ultimately real.
Thus we know that although the wisdom of the four teachings varies in depth, all are based upon the Four Noble Truths.
The section beginning with "Therefore" further cites two types of the Four Noble Truths from the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* to explain and establish the preceding meaning.

Regarding the "limited scope" of the Two Vehicles: because the *Zang* (Tripiṭaka) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings do not know the *tathāgatagarbha*, the Four Noble Truths they contemplate ultimately remain limited.
Because Bodhisattvas of the Separate and Perfect Teachings have realized the nature of the storehouse (ālaya), the Four Noble Truths they contemplate are all limitless.
Yet they also possess the finite, because the profound necessarily knows the shallow.
Other people contemplate and measure the immeasurable sequentially; those of perfect capacity (yuanren) contemplate the four sets of the Four Truths in a single thought-moment.
Second, from "The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra" (*Dajing*) onwards, it clarifies the commonality of causes and conditions.
All four wisdoms contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination; however, due to differences in the depth of their realization, there are four levels of attainment on the path to Bodhi.
Since that sutra uses the four wisdoms to manifest the meaning of the four teachings, we know that dependent origination is not restricted solely to the Hinayana.
II. From "Furthermore" onwards, it clarifies that [the Dharma] is solely great, in two parts:
first, it clarifies that it is exclusively the Dharma of Bodhisattvas; second, it cites a sutra.
Regarding the first: it cites a sutra.
Regarding "Māṇava": *māṇa* means benevolence (*ren*); thus, it refers to a benevolent and virtuous youth.
Regarding "practicing in accordance" (*xiying*): this means cultivating practice that accords with emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

As for the Four Truths and Dependent Origination, the first and last [terms] of each are cited while the middle ones are omitted; therefore, both are expressed as "down to the truths and conditions" (*zhendi yinyuan*).
Since this is the dharma corresponding to the bodhisattva of *dharmakṣānti*, it is verified that its principle is profound and beyond the reach of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

While that [realization] penetrates all three vehicles of the Mahāyāna, we now take the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*), wherein the correspondence between the truths and conditions constitutes the present wisdom of emptiness.
2. From "One should know" onwards, the conclusion is presented.
Second, explaining that the vision of the two vehicles is shallow, in three parts:
first, explaining the Śrāvakas.

If one considers them in terms of causes and conditions, the seven branches are collectively treated as a single *duḥkha* (suffering), and the five branches are likewise collectively treated as a single *samudaya* (origin).
Furthermore, the *duḥkha* and *samudaya* do not distinguish between the past and future; they are all entirely present.
Because their faculties are dull, the characteristics of the dharmas are presented in a general and abbreviated manner.
Second, the Pratyekabuddha is explained:
this opens up the general category of Śrāvakas to reveal their specific characteristics.
The five present factors are consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling.
The two future factors are birth and old age and death; these are the specific characteristics of suffering.
The two factors of the past refer to ignorance (*avidyā*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
The three factors of the present refer to craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*); this constitutes the collection according to their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, since the three time periods are opened up rather than being restricted to the present alone, it is said that by briefly indicating the results and briefly indicating the causes, the remaining three [factors] can be inferred from within.
Thus, all three periods of time each possess the twelve [links], and because merit serves as the support for wisdom, one is able to contemplate them individually.
Third, from "Although... onwards, there is the refutation of the shallow, which has two parts:
first, the direct refutation of the Two Vehicles.
The three trainings one cultivates are not for the sake of sentient beings, nor do they accomplish the Buddha-dharma; therefore, they are called "self-discipline" and "self-deliverance.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The precepts of the Two Vehicles are called self-discipline, meditative concentration is called self-deliverance, and wisdom is called self-purification."
Although Pratyekabuddhas possess a small measure of compassion, they cannot bring extensive benefit; therefore, they are likewise termed "self-centered.
Second, from "In contrast with Bodhisattvas" onwards, the text contrasts and highlights the Bodhisattva.
Not yet distinguishing between the provisional and the ultimate, these are merely Bodhisattvas, both of whom differ from the two vehicles.
Second, "Now, raising [the topic]" and below, clarifies that there are distinctions in the analysis of the essence; this has two parts:
first, clarifying the analytical contemplation (*vibhāvanā*) by way of what is common to the three vehicles.
Second, the contemplation of the essence by way of the unique qualities of the bodhisattva.

As clarified in various texts, the emptiness resulting from the analytical negation of what is substantially existent is called "analysis," whereas the fact that illusory existence is itself emptiness is termed "essence."

Now, it is clarified that the illusory existence itself is the Middle Way as its essence; therefore, both actual cessation and illusory emptiness are termed "analytical" (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), because they have not yet reached the true substance of all phenomena, and thus the meaning of "essence" is not established.
The term "due to" (*yī*) refers to the analytical meaning that all phenomena ultimately revert to impermanence.
Now, it is clarified that each and every phenomenon is eternally abiding; having seen the reality of phenomena, this is called the wondrous essence.
The first meaning is divided into two parts:
first, the individual explanation, which has two sections;
first, clarifying the contemplation with reference to the Two Vehicles, which has two sections:
First, the contemplation on the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā), in two parts:
first, drawing an analogy for investigation;
second, from "self and person" onwards, examining according to the phenomena (dharma).
Since each [aggregate] is individually non-existent, their combination is also non-existent; for a collection of empty space cannot constitute form.
Below the section "Identical with the Aggregates," he further examines both identity and difference to show that neither can be established.
2. From "Although he seeks" onwards is the contemplation on the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), which has two parts:
first, clarifying that phenomena persist.
This restates the preceding analogy to demonstrate that while the person perishes, the phenomenon persists.

"Fundamentally of itself" and below, clarifying that phenomena are themselves the Middle Way, in two [subsections]: 1. "Fundamentally of itself"
First, it clarifies that the nature is neither arising nor ceasing.
Through the three sections beginning with "originally," the Middle Way of this nature is revealed.

Regarding the phrase "originally there were no four great elements" (*mahābhūta*): this does not mean that the four great elements are entirely non-existent; rather, because these great aggregates are all the *tathāgatagarbha*, the substance of their nature is eternally abiding and fundamentally lacks the characteristic of arising. Therefore, it is said they are "originally non-existent."
Since there is no arising of phenomena, with what could they meet to form a conjunction?
Because there is no conjunction, there is nothing to be dispersed or extinguished; thus, emptiness is not a matter for debate.
In this way, the meaning within these words is made manifest.
2. From "originally itself" (*benzi*) onwards, it clarifies that it is not through contemplation that this state is achieved.

The characteristics of the world are primordially and eternally abiding; how could they only become non-arising and non-ceasing after one has stilled arising and ceasing through the wisdom of contemplation?
This name signifies that phenomena are identical to principle, and it is also said that the extremes are identical to the mean.
Second, the three phrases reveal [the truth] through contemplative understanding, in two parts:
first, the direct demonstration.
Although nature is fundamentally thus, delusion is dispelled through contemplation.

It is said that the practitioner's disposition is the cause and the teacher’s instruction is the condition; when cause and condition bring about contemplation, one penetrates the three truths of the fundamental nature.
The various great elements are themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle; therefore, they are non-arising from the very beginning.
Second, the citation of proof:
when ignorance is transformed, it changes into clarity, which is named the lamp of bodhi.
If it were not for the power of the causes and conditions of mutual response, how could ignorance be extinguished?
Thus we know that attaining Buddhahood is entirely dependent upon causes and conditions.
Third, from "Harmony" (*sāmagrī*) onwards, it clarifies that [the Buddha] is provisional while being identical to the Dharma; this has two parts:
First, establishing the fact that it contradicts reason;
second, from "This dharma" onwards, establishing the cultivation that illuminates the nature.
"Because this dharma exists" refers precisely to the cause and effect of delusion.
The phrase "the substance exists" refers to the three truths;
the phrase "is itself emptiness" refers to the three contemplations.
Both the objective realm and the contemplation arise through the conjunction of delusion and its causes and conditions.
2. From "The Three Contemplations" (*sanguan*) below, the contemplation is concluded.
Since these three sections of scripture correspond to the three contemplations, one knows that the present central tenet accords with the Buddha-mind; how could one not believe it?
2. From "Furthermore" (*gengwei*) onwards, [the text] addresses those of dull faculties (*mṛdv-indriya*) by once again refuting the clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).

Having previously explained emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and clarified the entry into the reality of phenomena (*dharmatā*), [the author notes that] while those of sharp faculties may already understand, there is fear that those of dull faculties might still be deluded. Therefore, the Great Master, out of his unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-karuṇā*), further explains its characteristics in two parts: first, the clarification of the clinging to phenomena; second, [the refutation thereof]. Regarding the first:
the clarification of the clinging to phenomena: [End of section]
First, the arising of views and attachment to the conditioned environment (*niśraya-vipāka*) has four parts.
First, the arising of the four attachments based on the great aggregates (*mahā-skandha*).
All non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and practitioners of the four teachings, as long as they have not yet suppressed or severed the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), all possess these attachments.
2. Below the section on the "Four Attachments," it is explained that the view of self arises from these four attachments.
Although among the four it is said that there is "non-existence" and "neither-nor," since they are all attachments, all four belong to the category of existence.
Since the view relies upon form (*rūpa*), it should correspondingly involve both the "self as distinct from form" (*rūpād anya ātmā*) and the "form as belonging to the self" (*ātmīyaṃ rūpam*).
Since the view relies upon the four aggregates (*skandha*), the same applies to both [the self as distinct from them and what belongs to the self].
Third, below the phrase "my birth," ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) arise based on the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).

Just as it is said that the four directions and downward movement arise from causes within space, so too do the ten afflictions (daśa-ānuśaya) give rise to birth and death. Even if one relies upon the Perfect Teaching’s doctrine of the inherent nature to open the four gates, if one clings to any single gate and gives rise to the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), then by giving rise to delusions and creating karma, one will invite future suffering; this is no different from the birth and death of those ordinary worldly people.
The Great Master is currently explaining the faults of the four attachments for the practitioner of the immediate path.
Second, from "This deludes" onwards, he points out that the mind of views is called the "defiled aggregates.
Since these five aggregates all constitute attachment and views, they are entirely defiled.
If the folding and unfolding [of phenomena] return to existence, how can they be called the emptiness of dharmas?
Second, from "The mind does not... onwards, the contemplation of emptiness is clarified in three parts:
first, clarifying that by not relying on this, one forgets the four attachments.
The mind does not rely upon the aggregates; this is true for all four teachings.

Now, to clarify the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong), regarding that which "does not rely," one takes the defiled aggregates themselves as the contemplating wisdom—what aggregate could there be to rely upon?
What attachment can be refuted?
Who is the one who contemplates?
Furthermore, there is nothing to be revealed.
The mind does not rely on the aggregates; now, I shall briefly explain the intent.
Second, from the phrase "tranquil" (*jiran*) onwards, it clarifies that by acceding to the principle, one is fully endowed with all virtues.

The three kinds of *prajñā* are non-dual and indistinguishable from the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* and the three bodies of the Muni; if one does not take these as the three contemplations, there would be no means by which they could be perceived.
3. Below the section on the "Practitioner," it is clarified that this contemplation can swiftly restore one to the original state.
The contemplation of arising and the contemplation of phenomena are both observed through the three contemplations within a single thought-moment, like carrying a precious jade in one's bosom.
Furthermore, regarding the principle of the *dharmatā* of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, it is as if returning to one’s original country;
within two or three lifetimes, one may ascend to the stage of perfection (*pariniṣpanna-vihāra*) and be able to maintain that realization.
Second, the explanation of the contemplation of the two emptinesses regarding the phenomena produced by the twelve links of dependent origination, in two parts:
First, the division of the text and establishment of the intent, in two parts:
first, the division of the text.
These twelve links are divided according to the phenomena of birth, following the sequence of this sutra text.
Since the first member is called "ignorance" (*avidyā*), and a name is merely a provisional designation, it belongs to the realm of arising phenomena.
Ignorance is the grasping at a self;
as the *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra* states, it is the "characteristic of calculating names."

In the subsequent passages, only "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) and so forth are mentioned; since "name" (*nāman*) is not mentioned, this is a direct reference to form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). This is because, from birth through to old age and death, nothing is produced apart from the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of form and mind.
Although the meaning is clear, one may still fear it is not believed; therefore, I cite the *Śāstra* (the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*) to provide proof for each section.
Regarding "Who is old and dies?": if one asks "Who?", the answer is "I"; thus we know that both "who" and "self" are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*).
The Sūtra says "is named," which accords in mystery with the Śāstra;
the Śāstra refers to it as "the emptiness of birth"—how could the Sūtra not be so?
That "this is old age and death" directly points to form and mind as the dharma of old age and death.
The Sūtra does not mention the term "name," which is consistent with the Śāstra.
Second, from "However, ten... onwards, the establishment of the thesis has two parts:
first, a general explanation of the characteristics of causes and conditions; second... [the rest of the text follows].
First, the heading and enumeration.
Second, the explanation, beginning with "The three periods," which has three parts;
the first concerns the three periods.
Regarding the refutation of the eternal self (*ātman*) in the past: since the past has already ceased, it is not eternal.
Regarding the refutation of the self in the present: since the five fruits are all a combination of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), there is no self.
Regarding those who will later destroy [the self] through nihilism: because there is a fruit in the future, it is not a total annihilation.
All who speak of the "self" (ātman) are outsiders who cling to the body and the self as being subject to such views as annihilationism or eternalism.
This meaning of the three periods of time is commonly transmitted by the world; thus, it is said to be what is used in ordinary practice.
Second, regarding retribution:
the former ten causal conditions belong to the present, while the latter two causal conditions belong to the future; these two periods together constitute the twelve [links].

As for the text stating "the beginning and end of one period," this refers to ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) being at the start of a single lifetime; it speaks of "beginning and end" in reference to their mutual association within that period, not implying they exist solely within a single world-age (*kalpa*).
These causes and conditions for the retribution are set forth in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*.

Because one exists within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the craving and affection generated toward the parents constitute ignorance (*avidyā*); the winds of inhalation and exhalation constitute formative action (*saṃskāra*); and from the stage of consciousness (*vijñāna*) onward, the meanings are identical to those of the three periods of time.
III. A Single Thought-moment, in two parts:
First, the teaching upon which it relies;
second, from "Like the eye" onwards, the clarification of its mode of activity, in two parts:
First, the direct explanation of the characteristics, in two parts:
first, the direct explanation in relation to objects.
Regarding "the six sense bases giving rise to greed": because the visual consciousness is defiled, it secretly draws along the other consciousnesses, each possessing a state of greed.
Therefore, the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra* states: "Because of craving for fragrance, the various consciousnesses become differentiated and become defiled and attached everywhere.
Regarding the phrase "in a single day" and so forth: when a single sense faculty encounters its object, twelve [consciousnesses] arise immediately.
The six sense faculties encounter their objects repeatedly day and night; what thought could fail to give rise to the twelve links of dependent origination?
Each link that forms a cause must necessarily experience its fruit; they revolve like a wheel and entangle like a net.
2. From "Now further" (*jin geng*) below, the arising of causes is further investigated.

Regarding the contemplation of causes and conditions as extending through the three periods of time, the intent is to investigate how past ignorance acts as the cause to produce present results, and upon these present results, afflictive causes arise once again.
The original intention was that ignorance would not arise even now; therefore, we now investigate how the characteristics of ignorance arise from the two locations of the past and the present.
The text has two parts:
first, the retrogressive investigation of past causes.
That which arises from name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is so stated because it is the beginning of the five fruits and because the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are already complete therein.
Since the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*) has not yet completed the five aggregates, it is not so mentioned.
The causes of the past culminate in ignorance (*avidyā*); observing ignorance now is intended to bring about the wisdom of full realization.

If one asserts that ignorance is definitively existent and so forth, then the wisdom capable of destroying it will instead become ignorance itself; thus the medicine becomes the disease. Therefore, it is said that all grasping within the four positions is ignorance. Since ignorance serves as a condition, how could it not give rise to mental formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the rest?
Regarding "as previously explained," the six sense bases through old age and death are all clarified as they were directly shown in the preceding text.
Second, from "furthermore, one contemplates" onwards, one traces back the present results in their proper order.
Regarding the phrase "within this feeling" (*vedanā*), it is because the limb of feeling is the conclusion of the five fruits that the contemplation reaches this point;
yet, if one generates attachment, it again becomes the twelve links of dependent origination within a single thought-moment.

"Or there may be those who receive [the results]" refers to the mind that lacks clarity due to ignorance; the factors such as volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are accomplished in a single moment.
Second, from "In this way" onwards, it is an expression of praise for the difficulty of knowing.

Whether examined through the process of retrogression or progression, although [the cycle] resides within a single thought-moment, its twelve links are perfectly complete; thus, the branches and twigs pervade all states of existence.
It is like a great tree that no one can even identify, let alone fell.

Regarding the "great tree," the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The two past links constitute the roots; the five present links constitute the trunk; the three present links constitute the flowers; and the two future links constitute the fruit."
Regarding "pervasive" (bùhù), the commentary on the *Wénxuǎn* states:
"Pervasive" describes the appearance of being extensive and abundant. It may be written with either the radical for speech (言) or the radical for water (水); both forms are correct.
The *Hanshu* states: "‘Buhuo’ (pervasive) is like ‘bulo’ (spread out); it means that they are spread everywhere, even in exposed places.
Second, regarding the section below "The Present Sūtra," there is a brief indication of the contemplative object (*ālambana*) of the present sūtra, in two parts:
first, clarifying the intent of the sūtra.

Regarding the practice of taking only the "arising phenomena" (utpāda-dharma) as the object: one takes the provisional designation of ignorance as the object for the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā), and takes the formations, consciousness, form, mind, and so forth as the object for the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā).
These two objects—causes and conditions—apply to the contemplations of all four teachings, yet here the intent lies in the Perfect Teaching (yuan).
2. From "It is appropriate to... below, the contemplation of the object is shown, in two parts:
first, showing the object, in two parts;
first, establishing a metaphor;
2. The Application of the Principle (*dharmasama*).

Those who cling to provisional names fail to penetrate the Three Truths and falsely give rise to the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), just as a whirling torch creates the illusion of a circle; therefore, it is said that [this clinging] does not cease.
The wheel exists dependent upon fire, yet it is provisionally named based on real dharmas as its cause.
Because of delusion, one fails to realize that form and mind are themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle; this is called being deluded regarding the aggregates and sense bases.
Regarding the phrase "firewood and fire," this refers to the embers.
Second, from "If one knows" onwards, the contemplation is demonstrated in two parts: first, establishing a simile; second, [the application of the simile]. (The second part follows below.)
Second, from "The Wheeling Fire" (*lun huo*) downward, the Dharma correspondence is established.

Contemplating arising and contemplating phenomena as being immediately empty, provisional, and middle constitutes the "Wheeling Fire" contemplation of the non-duality of both emptiness and the provisional.

2. From "The Emptiness of Beings" (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) below, the explanation of the text according to its meaning has two parts: first, delineating the characteristics of the objects; second, [the explanation of the subject].

First, delineating the characteristics of the objects has two parts: first, the object of the emptiness of beings; second, [the object of the emptiness of phenomena]. First, the object of the emptiness of beings... [text continues]
First, the division of the text;
second, the explanation of the meaning.
Since the first four [sections] explain them by means of the three contemplations of the emptiness of the preceding births, there is no commentary in the sub-commentary (*śū*).
2. From "the consciousness of formations" (*saṃskāra-vijñāna*) downward is the realm of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

There should likewise be three [aspects] for each: formations are themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle; and so on, up to old age and death being themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. The Buddha’s words are skillful and concise, as they can be inferred from the preceding examples.
2. From "The manifold sufferings" (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) onwards, the characteristics of the contemplation are presented in two parts:

first, the contemplation is demonstrated based on the scriptural text in two parts; first, the actual demonstration in two parts: 1. The actual demonstration: 2. [Subdivisions]... (as per original structure)
First, pointing to the text.
Second, from "the manifold sufferings" onwards, the explanation of the meaning, which has three parts:
first, clarifying the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*).
The various karmic activities of suffering refer to the dharmas that arise above.
Because their essence is wondrous, they are inconceivable.
Whether as arising or as dharmas, neither are empty nor existent; to realize this essence is called Madhyamaka (the Middle Way).

In this contemplation, one does not perceive a limit or a cessation in the cycle of birth and death; because it is the *dharmadhātu*, it is limitless, and because all things are eternally abiding, it is unceasing.
Second, from "originally non-existent" (*mūlataḥ abhāva*) onwards, the contemplation of emptiness is clarified.
3. Below "unwholesome," the contemplation of designation (jia guan) is clarified.
The previous unwholesome reflection constitutes the two past links;
the present unwholesome reflection constitutes the three present links.
"Practicing with a focused mind" refers to the aforementioned contemplation.
This is like raising a disease and necessarily applying its corresponding medicine; thus, the provisional observation is made manifest.

3. Regarding the passage "The Treatise says" below, the *dāna* (giving) encompasses the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).

The twelfth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains the perfection of giving, stating: "If a bodhisattva practices the perfection of giving and can thereby give rise to the other six perfections, at that time it is called the fulfillment of the perfection of giving."
How does giving give rise to the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*)?
There are three levels: inferior, middling, and superior.

Giving food, drink, and coarse material things with a gentle mind is called inferior. Being able to give clothing and precious objects is called middling generosity. Being able to give one's head, eyes, blood, flesh, kingdom, wealth, wife, and children is called superior.
What is giving that gives rise to the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*)?
The Bodhisattva reflects: "Sentient beings do not know how to practice giving; because they will be impoverished in future lives, they commit evil deeds.
If they were to practice giving, they would possess merit in future lives and lack nothing, whereby they would then be able to maintain ethical discipline."
What is the perfection of patience in arising?
When a bodhisattva practices giving, if the recipient insults them with abuse, or asks for much, or asks at an improper time, or asks for what should not be asked, the bodhisattva then reflects:
"I am now practicing giving with the desire to seek the Buddha-way."
"Furthermore, there is no one who compels me to practice giving; I do so for my own sake. Why, then, should I give rise to anger?
Having reflected thus, he practices patience.
What is the perfection of vigor?
When a bodhisattva practices giving, they constantly exercise vigor with the desire to practice the two kinds of giving, diligently seeking wealth and the Dharma to achieve fulfillment therein.
What is the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā) arising from birth?

When a bodhisattva practices giving, they are able to eliminate stinginess and greed while maintaining a single-minded focus, gradually removing the five hindrances; this is called the perfection of meditation.
Furthermore, the mind relies upon giving to enter the first dhyāna and even up to the meditative absorption of cessation.
How does this give rise to the perfection of wisdom?
When a bodhisattva practices giving, they know that there is a karmic fruit and harbor no doubt; thus, they are able to destroy wrong views and ignorance.
Furthermore, distinguishing between pure and impure giving results in different rewards; this is called the arising of wisdom.
Therefore, it is said that the meaning of *dāna* (generosity) subsumes the six perfections.

Although the other five perfections likewise mutually subsume one another, that is not the intent of the present text; thus, we shall discuss *dāna* alone, as it is the foremost of the six and is convenient for encompassing the arising [of the others].
